tier_reason: Independent third-party suite (NgFEP/NgFEP-assessment, an academic lab unaffiliated with GROMACS, NAMD or OpenMM) publishes run scripts, inputs (c-MD/*/..._inputs) and per-run raw ns/day .dat files for GROMACS, NAMD 3 and OpenMM 8.1 on 11 usable GPUs; every per-GPU mean in the record re-derives exactly from the .dat files. Not A because build, compiler, flags, CUDA/driver and host CPU models are not stated; held at B as an independent measurement although the suite is obscure (2 stars, no paper found) and has curation errors.

corrections.claimed_speedup: No project claim; independent measurement in NgFEP/NgFEP-assessment. Per-GPU means of 5 runs computed from the repo's .dat files (derived from page data), GROMACS 2023.3 (the repo writes 23.3) vs NAMD 3.0b5 vs OpenMM 8.1 in ns/day: A100 59.47 vs 39.19 vs 36.00 (1.52x NAMD, 1.65x OpenMM); RTX 4070 54.01 vs 22.46 vs 33.63 (2.40x, 1.61x); RTX A4500 30.85 vs 16.33 vs 21.58 (1.89x, 1.43x); RTX 2080 Ti 28.13 vs 14.25 vs 19.13 (1.97x, 1.47x; the OpenMM file is a byte-identical copy of the GP100 file); Quadro RTX 5000 21.07 vs 12.57 vs 16.39 (1.68x, 1.29x); Quadro RTX 6000 29.59 vs 17.92 vs 23.51 (1.65x, 1.26x); Quadro GP100 22.22 vs 15.23 vs 19.13 (1.46x, 1.16x); RTX 3090 33.03 vs 23.40 vs 26.96 (1.41x, 1.23x); P100 19.69 vs 14.66 vs 13.69 (1.34x, 1.44x); GTX 1080 Ti 15.26 vs 11.80 vs 11.78 (1.29x, 1.30x); V100 25.13 vs 24.26 vs 22.54 (1.04x, 1.11x). Across the 11 GPUs with complete data GROMACS is 1.04x to 2.40x NAMD and 1.11x to 1.65x OpenMM (derived from page data). AMBER 22 pmemd.cuda in the same suite is faster than GROMACS on 5 of these 11 GPUs (up to 1.47x on V100, 36.89 vs 25.13 ns/day, derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: The wave 8 categories have no molecular-dynamics bucket; geometry-spatial (cell and neighbour lists) was kept from the lead's guess and the orchestrator may override. LAMMPS, a listed baseline, is not in this benchmark and no reachable page compares GROMACS with LAMMPS (arXiv, manual.gromacs.org, mdbench.ace-net.ca and the published GROMACS papers were EGRESS_BLOCKED). The suite (NgFEP/NgFEP-assessment, 2 stars, no licence file, one author, no paper found) is independent of all three codes but is not a well-known shootout. The comparison is not like for like: GROMACS uses V-rescale plus Parrinello-Rahman, NAMD Langevin plus Langevin piston, OpenMM Langevin plus a Monte Carlo barostat every 25 steps; run lengths differ (nsteps 10000 for GROMACS, 100000 for NAMD and OpenMM); NAMD ran a 3.0b5 beta build with +p1 (one CPU thread) while GROMACS used 4 OpenMP threads with bonded forces on the CPU; OpenMM picks its PME grid from ewaldErrorTolerance 0.0004 instead of the fixed 144^3 grid; ns/day is parsed from three different log formats, and OpenMM's figure is wall time around sim.step including reporter output. Constraints are equivalent (NAMD 'rigidBonds all' constrains bonds to hydrogen plus rigid water, matching GROMACS h-bonds and OpenMM HBonds). Curation errors in the data: the OpenMM GP100 and RTX 2080 Ti .dat files are byte-identical, so one of those OpenMM rows is a copy; the GTX 1080 Ti GROMACS _1 and _8 files are byte-identical and the plotting notebook uses the _4 file (mean 15.26 vs 14.60 ns/day for the other two, which would give 1.24x NAMD); the TITAN V GROMACS file holds a single 0 (failed run) and is excluded. The same suite's AMBER 22 pmemd.cuda (not OSI-licensed; run on a 128^3 PME grid) is faster than GROMACS on 5 of 11 GPUs (V100 36.89 vs 25.13 ns/day, RTX 3090 43.42 vs 33.03, Quadro RTX 6000 31.83 vs 29.59, RTX 2080 Ti 28.97 vs 28.13, P100 20.07 vs 19.69) and level on Quadro RTX 5000, so GROMACS is not the fastest code on this page. GROMACS '23.3' in the repo is release 2023.3, not the newest. Absolute numbers look untuned next to MDBench (WebSearch snippet only: GROMACS 2023.2 on one Narval A100 at 88.4 ns/day on 6n4o, against 59.5 here); MDBench (Digital Research Alliance of Canada) is a well-known independent suite with GROMACS, NAMD3, PMEMD and OpenMM runs on the same 6n4o system and is the better source for a retier where mdbench.ace-net.ca is reachable. The V100 row (1.04x NAMD) shows the lead is GPU-generation dependent.

notes: All record numbers re-derive exactly from the raw .dat files; metadata checked (966 stars, LGPL-2.1-or-later per COPYING and source headers, last commit 2026-10-06, not a fork). Record's caveat that NAMD's 'rigidBonds all' differs from GROMACS h-bonds was wrong and is corrected; new shortcomings: copied OpenMM data file (GP100 = RTX 2080 Ti), GTX 1080 Ti file selection, AMBER 22 beats GROMACS on 5 of 11 GPUs in the same suite, numbers below MDBench. Orchestrator may retier to C if 'well-known suite' is read strictly; category override to a non-geometry bucket is likely needed.

tier_reason: PlayCanvas engine PR #9581 shows a table of ms per RigidBodyComponentSystem#step(1/60) for Jolt vs Ammo.js (Bullet compiled to WebAssembly) matching every number in the record, but gives no CPU, no Ammo.js or Node version, no flags and no benchmark script link; it is a third-party PR, not a benchmark suite, and Jolt's own multicore whitepaper (jrouwe.nl) could not be opened, so C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Jolt: the single-threaded wasm build from the jolt-physics 1.1.0 npm package (vendored in examples/assets/wasm/jolt of the PR). Ammo.js build and version, Node.js version and compiler flags not stated.
corrections.workload: Rigid-body step time in ms per physics step (RigidBodyComponentSystem#step(1/60)) for 400 boxes or boxes and spheres dropped on a floor, run in Node.js, minimum of 5 runs, Jolt (single-threaded WebAssembly build from jolt-physics 1.1.0 npm) against Ammo.js inside the PlayCanvas engine.
corrections.caveats: The numbers come from a third-party pull request (PlayCanvas engine PR #9581 by willeastcott, opened 2026-09-28 and still open on 2026-10-07) that adds Jolt as a physics backend, not from Jolt's author. It names Node.js, 400 bodies and 'minimum of 5 runs' and says it uses the single-threaded wasm build from the jolt-physics 1.1.0 npm package, but gives no CPU, no Ammo.js or Node versions, no compiler or flags and no link to the benchmark script, so it is tier C. Both engines run as single-threaded WebAssembly, which says little about native C++ Jolt against native Bullet and does not exercise Jolt's multicore design. The headline win is mostly the sleeping case (settled bodies cost almost nothing in Jolt); while bodies are colliding Jolt is slower or level in 3 of 5 scenes, and the PR says Jolt's own step is about 20% slower than Ammo's (4.94 ms with no contact listener), with the per-contact callback adding about 0.8 ms. The stronger primary source is Jolt's own whitepaper 'Jolt Physics Multicore Scaling' (https://jrouwe.nl/jolt/JoltPhysicsMulticoreScaling.pdf, linked from the README and Docs/PerformanceTest.md; the repo ships the PerformanceTest app that produces such numbers), which compares Jolt's scaling with other engines; jrouwe.nl was EGRESS_BLOCKED again, so its numbers were not read, and a retier in an environment that can open it could reach A or B. Discussion #327 shows Pierre Terdiman's PEEL runs against PhysX 4.1.2 and 5.1.0 on an Intel i9 where the curves intersect and match once settings are aligned, so there is no single winner. Issue #1081 (opened 2024-04-29, closed, resolution not visible) reports Jolt tick times above 200 ms with 10k-20k static colliders where PhysX 4/5 and Bepu Physics 2 stay under 5 ms with 2 million, a workload where Jolt was far slower. The wave 8 categories have no physics-engine bucket; geometry-spatial (broad phase and collision) was chosen over the lead's guessed blas-lapack and the orchestrator may override. The lead's baseline 'ODE or Bullet' leaves ODE untested.

notes: Numbers in the record match the PR table exactly and its derived ratios are correct; metadata checked (11.7k stars, MIT, last commit 2026-10-04, not a fork or archived). Shortcomings: WASM-only, single-threaded, mixed result (Jolt slower while colliding), no hardware or versions for Ammo, open PR; Jolt's whitepaper on jrouwe.nl is the needed source for a retier. Category is a poor fit (no physics bucket).
